en: The definition of pervasion according to the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin).

The definition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) according to the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) is: "not occurring in that which possesses the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavat*). Fire is the probandum; a lake is that which possesses its absence; the occurrence [of smoke] in fish, moss, and so forth is found there, while its non-occurrence is found in smoke—thus is the application of the definition. The refined meaning is: pervasion is the state of not occurring as determined by that which possesses the absence of the probandum.

Even when this has been stated, because of the cognition that "fire does not exist in the kitchen by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*)," the kitchen possesses the absence of fire, and smoke indeed exists in it; thus, there is the fault of over-narrowness (*avyāpti*). To exclude this, the qualification "being delimited by the relation that delimits the probandum-ness (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha*)" is added to the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) residing in the probandum. This being the case, since fire is intended to be proved on the mountain by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), the relation that delimits the probandum-ness is conjunction.

Therefore, since there is no absence whose counter-positiveness resides in the probandum (sādhya) as delimited by the relation of conjunction in the kitchen, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti). Even when this is stated—given the cognition that "there is a fire from the crossroads in the kitchen" (according to the *cālanī* maxim)—one might establish the absence of fire in the kitchen and then claim that smoke exists therein, which would again result in a lack of pervasion. To prevent this, the qualification "delimited by the delimitor of the probandumhood" (*sādhyatāvacchedakāvacchinnatva*) is introduced into the counter-positiveness. This being so, since there is no absence in the kitchen whose counter-positiveness is delimited by the property of fireness (*vahnitva*), there is no lack of pervasion.

Even when this has been stated, in the valid reason (saddhetu) "this tree is in contact with a monkey because it is this very tree," there is non-pervasion (avyāpti). This is because the absence of contact exists in the tree—since contact exists in the tree by way of the relation of inherence (samavāya)—and thus the tree possesses an absence whose counter-positive-ness (pratiyogitā) is delimited by the nature of contact and restricted by the relation of inherence; yet the [reason] "being this very tree" (etadvṛkṣatva) indeed subsists in that [tree]. To exclude this, the qualification "having a different locus from the counter-positive" (pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa) is introduced for the absence. And here, "having a different locus" means subsisting in what is not the locus of that [counter-positive].

By the word "that" (tat), the monkey-conjunction to be proven is grasped. Its locus is this tree; its non-locus is a quality (guṇa). The absence residing therein is the absence of conjunction. The state of not residing in that [quality] exists in "this-treeness" (etadvṛkṣatva); thus, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti).

Even so, there is again the fallacy of under-extension (*avyāpti*) because of the cognition: "By way of conjunction, there is no conjunction with a monkey in this tree. This implies that the absence of conjunction with a monkey exists in this tree-ness, and its occurrence (*tadvṛttitva*) resides in this tree-ness. To exclude this, the qualification "being delimited by the relation that delimits the counter-positivehood" (*pratiyogitāvacchedakasambandhāvacchinnatva*) is applied to the locus-membership (*ādheyatā*) residing in the counter-positive. And that relation is precisely the relation that delimits the probandumhood (*sādhyatāvacchedakasambandha*).

And thus, the definition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established as follows: it is the absence of occurrence (*vṛttitvābhāva*) in that which possesses an absence (*abhāva*) which is non-co-located with its counter-positive (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*), where the counter-positive has a location characterized by inherence (*samavāya-sambandha-avacchinna-adheyatā*) and a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and delimited by inherence (*samavāya-sambandha-avacchinna*).

By this, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of "this tree is not [a tree]," because the counter-positive—which possesses a location characterized by inherence—is not co-located with the locus.

By this [definition] as well, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of "being a universal (*jāti*)" with respect to "possessing qualified existence" (*viśiṣṭasattvavattva*), because it is deviant (*vyabhicārin*). To explain: the probandum (*sādhya*) is qualified existence. According to the principle that "the qualified and the pure are non-different," existence itself is the probandum. Since universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth lack that [existence], and yet universality resides in them, it follows that being pervaded by existence (*sattāvyāpyatva*) would apply to universals; thus, there is over-extension. To exclude this, the qualification "delimited by the delimitor of the counter-correlativity" (*pratiyogitāvacchedakāvacchinnatva*) is applied to the locusness (*ādheyatā*) residing in the counter-correlate.

This being the case, since a quality (*guṇa*) is a locus of an absence whose counter-positive does not reside in that which possesses the substratehood delimited by "qualified existence" (*viśiṣṭasattātva*), it follows that [the definition] applies to the genus (*jāti*); for while the genus indeed resides in that [quality], it does not fail to reside there. Thus, over-extension (*ativyāpti*) is avoided.

By this much, the definition is established as follows: pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the absence of residence in the reason (*hetu*), as characterized by an absence residing in that which does not have as its locus a counter-positive delimited by a relation that delimits the counter-positiveness of an absence whose counter-positiveness is itself delimited by the delimitor of the probandumness (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*), and where that counter-positiveness is not delimited by a relation other than conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Even so, in the case of "the mountain possesses fire because of smoke," there exists an absence of fire that is counter-correlative to fire and non-co-locative with fire—namely, the absence of fire residing in the parts of the smoke. Since the smoke-part possesses that [absence], and the smoke possesses the property of being resident in it, there is an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) even in the case of a valid reason (*saddhetu*). To exclude this, the qualification "being delimited by the relation that delimits the probanshood" (*hetutāvacchedakasambandhāvacchinnatva*) is added to the property of residence. In the present case, since smoke exists in the subject (*pakṣa*) by way of the relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), the relation that delimits the probanshood is conjunction.

The subsistence residing in smoke, as determined by the parts of smoke, is delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*); therefore, subsistence as delimited by the relation that delimits the state of being a reason (*hetutāvacchedaka-sambandha*) is not determined by the parts of smoke. Thus, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*).

Even with this much stated, there is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), such as "smoke-possessing [is] because of fire. For example: the absence defined by the locus of the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*), which has as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) the property of residing [in that locus], is the absence established by the cognition "there is neither residence nor a pot in the iron ball (*ayogolaka*). Therefore, since the definition of non-pervasion—consisting in the absence of residence defined by a locus possessing an absence whose counter-positive is non-co-referential with the counter-positive of the probandum—is present in "fire," there is over-extension.

To prevent that [over-extension], the qualification "being delimited by the property of being a locus-ness" (*vṛttitvatvāvacchinnatva*) must be added. Consequently, since the cognition "there is no locus-ness residing in fire in the iron ball" (*ayogolaka*) is established, the absence whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the property of being a locus-ness residing in fire does not exist; thus, the definition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not applicable there, and there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

As for the argument that an absence whose counter-correlativity is locus-ness is established in the iron ball by taking the absence of both fire and pot—this is not a fault, because it is an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the duality of both locus-ness and pot-ness (*vṛttitvaghaṭobhayatvāvacchinnapratiyogitāka*).
